#### 启动与依赖

| 依赖或条件 | 是否必需 | 用途 | 缺失或不满足时 |
|---|---|---|---|
| DSH MCP client与stdio服务 | 接入必需 | 启动mcp-rea | 无握手则无可用工具 |
| setup生成的镜像shim | bundle行必需 | HOME下真实入口 | 首次未供给时模块不存在 |
| 符合manifest的Node/REA | 必需 | 运行CLI和MCP | 显式system无可用REA则失败 |
| JDK/Ghidra等引擎 | 特定工具必需 | 上游分析 | doctor列unmet不等于整体不可启动 |
| 网络、磁盘与解压工具 | 供给时条件 | 取得组件 | offline缺REA则拒绝安装 |

#### 成本

| 阶段 | 现金与资源成本 | 人工与时间投入 | 已知条件与未知项 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 首次使用 | 多组件下载/磁盘和模型费用未知 | 探针、代理、解压和版本处理 | 复用是否可行取决于环境 |
| 持续使用 | REA进程与引擎资源未知 | 对齐包/镜像/bundle/system状态 | auto可能改变实际REA |
| 失败恢复 | 重新供给或独立环境资源未知 | 读锁/日志、重跑setup、查残留 | 后台开始不等于MCP就绪 |

#### 效果

| 效果项 | 当前证据支持 | 尚不能确定 |
|---|---|---|
| 集中供给 | manifest、setup和bundle状态写入 | 平台完整成功率与耗时 |
| MCP接入 | patch与shim真实spawn链 | 目标工具可用与结果正确 |
| 诊断 | mode/unmet/重复注册等信息 | 是否降低实际排障负担 |
启动选择与镜像回退显式报告，ignore-scripts和offline拒绝路径说明供给边界；Windows进程树和多层状态仍是移植代价。[Q03](#research-q03)
把REA及其依赖供给、路径记录、镜像启动和DSH行配置组织起来，使接入状态可检查；逆向核心能力归上游，并未因此获得新算法。[Q01](#research-q01)
auto可委派系统REA，doctor的probe ok仍可有unmet，Windows强杀又可能留下进程；包钉子不等于任务运行栈固定或所有工具可用。[Q03](#research-q03)
任务级实际启动与引擎就绪清单可能提高环境漂移后的复现，需与现有status对比排障时间和维护负担；尚未实现。[Q04](#research-q04)

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-plugin-rea?style=flat-square&color=cb3837)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-plugin-rea)

**English** · [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md)

> **Which version is this? 2.x — and `main` is it.** 2.x provisions the runtime itself (Node, the REA CLI, a
> JDK, Ghidra) and then wires the row: install the plugin, run `scripts/setup.mjs` once, restart dsh.
> **1.x** is the older configuration-only adapter — it expects `rea` on PATH and Ghidra installed by you —
> kept on the [`v1` branch](https://github.com/czcdr/dsh-plugin-rea/tree/v1) and on npm as `dsh-plugin-rea@1.0.6`.
> Full comparison: [Two lines: 1.x and 2.x](#two-lines-1x-and-2x) · upgrading: [Upgrading from 1.x](#upgrading-from-1x).

> REA **6.8.0** — this package's pin — still accepts Ghidra **12.1.x** only (12.2 is `unsupported`, and the whole
> Ghidra decompile/analysis group disappears) and the jadx bridge **0.7.1** only (0.8.0 fails on its first call with
> `Expected engine 0.7.1`, before any APK is loaded). Both gates were re-checked against 6.8.0 on 2026-10-26 and
> neither one moved. JDK **21.0.13** is out upstream, but Adoptium publishes no Windows build of it, so there is
> nothing to point at here — and it drops only three of the four eMudhra anchors. The trade-off is therefore "all
> tools green, CVE still open": Ghidra 12.1.4's CVE-2026-100504 / 100505 / 100503 / 113604 stay in the chain — **do
> not analyse untrusted samples with this environment** — and the JDK still trusts the eMudhra anchors. Evidence,
> mitigations and revisit triggers: [docs/update-review-2026-10-24.md](docs/update-review-2026-10-24.md) and
> [docs/update-review-2026-10-26.md](docs/update-review-2026-10-26.md).
>
> **Ghidra 12.2 itself works** — measured 2026-10-26: same 9 segments, same 341 procedures, byte-identical `entry`
> pseudocode as 12.1.4, through REA's own bridge. What blocks it is REA's version-equality check, not the bridge.
> If you want the CVE-fixed engine anyway, `node scripts/ghidra-gate-override.mjs --enable --version 12.2` rewrites
> that one constant in the vendored copy, records what it changed in `<bundle>/ghidra-gate-override.json`, and
> `--disable` restores it; re-running setup reverts it too. It needs **JDK 25+** (`application.java.min=25`).

> **You must run `node scripts/setup.mjs` yourself — once after installing, and once after every plugin
> upgrade.** Nothing runs it for you: a market install or update replaces the package and stops there.
> Since **2.0.8** a market upgrade keeps the *row* working (the mirrored launcher re-execs the new one), but it
> does **not** move the bundle to the new pins — REA and the engines stay at the versions recorded by the last
> setup run. Skip it on a first install and the row exits `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` with no tools and no message;
> skip it after an upgrade and you keep running the old REA silently (`check-updates.ps1` reports the drift).
> If you had enabled the Ghidra gate override (see §9 of the 2026-10-26 review), that setup run re-provisions the
> bundled REA and the patch goes with it — re-enable it afterwards, or accept the pinned Ghidra again.
> The full rule set is under [Updating](#updating--three-independent-things).

> **A first install and every plugin upgrade also show a one-time guide in the Web GUI.** It says whether the
> runtime is missing or behind this package's pin, shows the exact `node "<install path>/scripts/setup.mjs"`
> command for that install, and remembers the dismissal per plugin version. It is a notice only: it never runs
> setup for you and never edits the bundle. Run it once, restart dsh, and the guide stays away until the next
> plugin version.

Brings the upstream **[REA — Reverse Engineer Anything](https://github.com/morluto/rea)** MCP server into
**DeepSeek Harness** (dsh), so its tools show up in a session as `mcp__rea__*`.

![dsh-plugin-rea: the session calls the official MCP client row, which launches the bundle's shim; the shim starts the provisioned REA and the Evidence comes back](assets/screenshot-1.png)

## What this is

A **Cordis bundle with a provisioning layer**. `package.json` declares `dsh.bundle.patch`, and that patch
inserts one row of the official MCP client plugin (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client`). The row launches
`bin/rea-shim.mjs` with the running Node executable; the shim reads the machine-local state that
`scripts/setup.mjs` wrote and starts the REA CLI it provisioned. There is no analysis code here, and the
published patch contains no machine path.

> **Third-party adapter.** This repository is not part of REA, ships none of REA's code, and is not
> maintained by REA's authors. It composes one configuration row and fetches upstream's own releases.
> Upstream: [github.com/morluto/rea](https://github.com/morluto/rea) (MIT) ·
> [docs](https://github.com/morluto/rea#what-you-can-analyze) ·
> [rea.tools](https://rea.tools/) · npm package `rea-agents`.
> REA's own problems go to its tracker; **this plugin's** problems go to
> [this repository's issues](https://github.com/czcdr/dsh-plugin-rea/issues).

**It adds exactly three things:** the tool registration under the `mcp__rea__*` names, the per-machine
engine environment (`GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR`, `JAVA_HOME`, `REA_ADB_PATH`, `REA_APKTOOL_COMMAND`,
`REA_JADX_MCP_JAR`, `REA_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE`, …) scoped to that MCP child instead of the whole harness, and
the provisioning that puts those components on disk.

## What it can and cannot do

The analysis is upstream's; this section only restates upstream's own contract so expectations are right.

- **It cannot recover complete source code.** For native binaries upstream returns *pseudocode and
  assembly*, for Android APKs *decompiled methods*, for JEB units *pseudocode*, and for JavaScript/Electron
  *modules and their relations*. Upstream's tool contract states the pseudocode "is decompiler output, not
  original source and not text-equivalent" to another provider's output.
- Not recoverable in practice: original identifier names, types, comments, macros and template expansion,
  build scripts and assets. Optimisation (inlining, reordering), symbol stripping, obfuscation, packing and
  VM protection only make the output worse.
- Every result carries **confidence and limitations** (`observed` / `derived` / `inferred`, plus an explicit
  limitations list). Read them as evidence, never as recovered source.
- Good for: understanding behaviour, locating an implementation, interoperability and compatible
  re-implementation, security review, migration reference. To obtain actual source code, use the legitimate
  route — the upstream repository, vendor authorisation, or the vendor's own SDK.

**What provisioning cannot buy you.** These are upstream host gates, not settings this plugin forgot:

| Capability | Gate |
|---|---|
| Hopper provider | macOS only |
| IDA provider | needs your own IDA and `REA_IDA_MCP_CONFIG`; REA never launches IDA |
| firmware `binwalk` / `unblob` | Linux only |
| Wakaru JS recovery, pwntools ELF/recorded-crash paths | Linux x64 only |
| pwndbg / gdb core context | Linux, macOS |
| native mitmproxy captures | Linux (`REA_MITMDUMP_COMMAND`); HAR needs no engine |
| Apple toolchain (Mach-O, plist, asset catalog, LLDB) | macOS only |
| `capture_process_scenario` | Linux/macOS PTY |
| apktool (Android resource decoding) | available only when `REA_APKTOOL_COMMAND` points at something Node can **execute directly**: upstream `execFile`s that command without a shell, and Windows cannot execute a `.bat`/`.cmd` that way (EINVAL). This bundle wires the official `apktool.bat` as upstream documents, so on Windows the launcher reports no version and the capability stays unavailable; JADX (a jar) is unaffected |

## Two lines: 1.x and 2.x

| | **2.x** — this line, `main` | **1.x** — [`v1`](https://github.com/czcdr/dsh-plugin-rea/tree/v1) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | the adapter **plus provisioning**: it prepares Node, the REA CLI, a JDK and Ghidra, then wires the row | configuration-only adapter: one MCP row pointing at a `rea` you installed yourself |
| What you need first | nothing for the runtime — provisioning fetches what is missing (with `--reuse` it adopts an existing Ghidra/JDK instead) | Node.js on REA's engines, `npm i -g rea-agents`, and Ghidra 12.1.x for native analysis |
| First run | run `scripts/setup.mjs` (or the bootstrap) once, then restart dsh | nothing to run |
| The row launches | the running Node executable plus `<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/rea-shim.mjs`, which reads that machine's state | `cmd.exe /c rea mcp` on Windows, `rea mcp` on macOS/Linux |
| Machine state | `<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/` — `bundle.json`, `vendor/`, `cache/` | your own REA and Ghidra installs |
| Install | `dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-plugin-rea` (npm `latest` ≥ 2.0.0) | `… add dsh-plugin-rea@1.0.6`, or `github:czcdr/dsh-plugin-rea#v1.0.6` |

Both lines ship the **same patch shape** — one `insert` row of `@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client` — and offer the
same `mcp__rea__*` surface; they differ in who prepares the runtime. Moving from 1.x to 2.x takes two
commands: see [Upgrading from 1.x](#upgrading-from-1x).

Upstream also registers itself with dsh now (`rea setup --client dsh`); that route is essentially the
1.x model maintained upstream — configuration only, your own Node/REA/Ghidra. This bundle is the
zero-dependency route. Pick one of the three, and never keep two `serverName: rea` rows at once.

## Install

**Nothing to install first.** On a bare Windows x64 machine:

```
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\rea-bundle-bootstrap.ps1 -Reuse
```

`-Reuse` adopts a Ghidra/JDK you already have; omit it to download both (about 775 MB from the official
releases, checksum-verified). Then install the plugin for your profile:

```
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-plugin-rea
# or pin this release instead of tracking npm latest:
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add github:czcdr/dsh-plugin-rea#v2.0.13
```

> **On an Electron host (the DeepSeek Harness desktop app) the profile is owned by the application.**
> `dsh plugin --profile desktop …` is refused by the CLI (`profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by
> the Electron application`) — install or update through the in-app plugin manager instead. The CLI form
> above is for a profile you created yourself with the CLI under another name.

If Node is already installed, you can skip the bootstrap and run provisioning directly:

```
node scripts/setup.mjs --reuse      # or --dry-run to see the plan first
```

Node, when you provide it instead of letting setup fetch one, must satisfy REA's engines —
`^22.23.4 || ^24.22.1 || >=26.12.1` (check with `node -v`). REA raised those floors in 6.8.0: the pinned
24.22.1 is now the *oldest* acceptable 24.x, so a 24.11–24.21 runtime that 6.7.0 accepted is rejected here.
A lower Node does not fail at install time; the MCP row fails later, which reads as silence.

Installing the plugin **first** also works, but it takes two steps. The row resolves to
`<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/rea-shim.mjs`, and that file is created by setup — so until the first
provisioning run the row exits with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, and nothing is there to start a background
provisioning (the harness itself is unaffected: `failOnStartupError: false` is deliberate). Run
`node scripts/setup.mjs` once; from then on the shim is in place, and every later missing state is picked up
by the shim itself, which provisions in the background.

### Which DSH versions

`package.json` declares `engines.dsh: ">=0.1.7-rc.2 <0.3.0-0"`, and that declaration is the answer the plugin market
reads: with it the card says **compatible**; without it the market can only say *unknown*. The range is not a guess —
it is the dsh release list this plugin is checked against, and `node scripts/host-compat.mjs` fails the build when the
two disagree:

| Host | Covered |
|---|---|
| `0.1.7-rc.2` … `0.2.1-rc.2` — every release in between, alpha and rc | yes |
| `0.3.0` and later | no — a new minor line is a host nobody updated this row for yet |

What was actually compared across that range is the row provider: `packages/mcp/mcp-client` at `dsh-v0.1.7-rc.2` and at
`dsh-v0.2.1-rc.2` exposes the same config surface the shipped row uses (`serverName`, `transport`, `command`, `args`,
`env`, `failOnStartupError`), and `dsh.bundle.patch` exists at both tags. A host outside the range can still work; it is
simply not claimed.

### A REA you already have is used as-is

2.x exists to supply what a machine is missing. If REA is already installed — `rea` on PATH, the 1.x setup — the row
runs **that**, exactly as the 1.x line did, and nothing is provisioned:

| What the machine has | What the row runs |
|---|---|
| `rea` on PATH, at least as new as the provisioned build | your REA (`rea mcp`), with your Node and your PATH |
| `rea` on PATH but older than the provisioned build | the provisioned bundle — a stale global CLI would take the tool count backwards (6.4.0 ships 170 tools, 6.7.0 ships 207, 6.8.0 ships 229) |
| no `rea` on PATH | the provisioned bundle, provisioning itself on first use |

- `REA_BUNDLE_LAUNCH=auto|system|bundle` overrides the decision (`auto` is the default); `REA_BUNDLE_SYSTEM_REA=<path>`
  names a binary that is not on PATH.
- The probe is the CLI's own `--version`, bounded at 8 s: a `.cmd` shim on Windows takes ~2.4 s to answer, so the check
  runs once per start and only when a `rea` actually exists.
- `--shim-status` prints the decision — `launch.mode`, `launch.reason`, `launch.systemRea` — and its `launch.rejected`
  list says why a candidate was skipped (`"exit 7"`, `"inside the bundle"`, `"timeout"`).
- A delegated child carries `REA_BUNDLE_DELEGATED=1`, so a wrapper that calls this shim cannot make it delegate to
  itself forever.
- **On Windows a forced kill of the shim does not reap the delegated REA.** There is no job object here: Task Manager
  or a supervisor terminating the shim leaves your `rea` running with the row's pipes (a console Ctrl+C reaches the
  whole process group and does stop it). On POSIX the child is in the same group and dies with the terminal.

## Configure — nothing

The shipped row carries **no machine path**:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: mcp-rea
      name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client'
      config:
        serverName: rea
        transport: stdio
        command: !!js process.execPath
        args:
          - !!js "(process.env.DSH_HOME && process.env.DSH_HOME.trim() !== '' ? process.env.DSH_HOME : (process.env.USERPROFILE || ((process.env.HOMEDRIVE || '') + (process.env.HOMEPATH || '')) || process.env.HOME || '') + '/.dsh') + '/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/rea-shim.mjs'"
          - mcp
        env:
          ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE: '1'
        failOnStartupError: false
```

Three details in that row are load-bearing, and all three were bugs first:

- **The `!!js` scalar is quoted.** A bare scalar containing `? ` and `: ` is not one scalar: YAML reads it as an explicit key/value pair, so the loader receives a *mapping* where an expression belongs. Measured against the harness's own dialect (`JSON_SCHEMA` plus the `!!js` type from `app.asar`), the unquoted form made `args[0]` into `{"[object Object]": "..."}` — an object the row cannot launch with. Quoting removes the ambiguity, and the JS string literals inside then use single quotes.
- **Forward slashes, never backslashes.** A single-quoted YAML scalar keeps `\` literal, and JavaScript then consumes it: `'\plugins'` is not a path but the BEL control character, `'\rea-bundle'` becomes a carriage return and `'\bin'` a backspace — the path is destroyed silently. Forward slashes work on Windows and on POSIX.
- **The `DSH_HOME` fallback is `<home>/.dsh`, not `<home>`.** The shim, `setup.mjs` and `bootstrap.ps1` all resolve an unset `DSH_HOME` to `<home>/.dsh/...`; a fallback that stopped one level higher made the row point at a file provisioning never writes — invisible on any machine where `DSH_HOME` happens to be set.
- **The home fallback mirrors `os.homedir()`: `USERPROFILE`, then `HOMEDRIVE`+`HOMEPATH`, then `HOME`.**
  The middle pair is what a Windows service account gets instead of `USERPROFILE`; an expression that skipped
  it produced `/.dsh/...` — the root of the current drive — for exactly the accounts that cannot read that
  path. Only when all four are empty (a container account with no home at all) does the concatenation land on
  `/.dsh/...`, and `failOnStartupError: false` keeps that quiet, so the only symptom is "no `mcp__rea__*`
  tools". Set `DSH_HOME` explicitly on such an account.
- **No `path`/`require` in a `!!js` expression**: `ctx` is the loader scope, so the DSH_HOME fallback is written as plain concatenation.

`npm run bundle:audit` enforces the first three: it evaluates this exact expression with `DSH_HOME` unset, empty and set, and rejects a bare scalar that YAML would read as a mapping.

`ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` only matters if the harness itself runs on Electron; it is harmless for a plain Node host, and stating it explicitly beats relying on it surviving the child-env scrub.

`command` is the running Node executable and `args[0]` is computed from `DSH_HOME`, so the same patch works
on Windows, macOS and Linux without a PATH entry. Everything machine-specific lives in
`<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/bundle.json`, written by setup and readable with:

```
node bin/rea-shim.mjs --shim-status      # resolved paths, versions, verification state
node bin/rea-shim.mjs --shim-print-env   # the environment the MCP child will see
```

Both commands answer with the same bundle whether you run them from the plugin directory (the checkout copy)
or from `<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle` (the mirrored copy): the checkout resolves the location by the same
rule setup uses, while the mirror uses its own position — it cannot rely on `DSH_HOME`, which the harness
strips from an MCP child's environment.

Setting `REA_BUNDLE_AUTO_PROVISION=0` disables the first-run background provisioning.

To pin a different launch command on this machine (for example your own globally installed `rea`), override
the row from the profile's own `cordis.patch.yml` — that file is machine-local and never published. Only one
row may use `serverName: rea` in a profile.

A patch replaces the row's `config` **wholesale** — it does not deep-merge — so a partial override such as
`config: {env: {...}}` also deletes `command`, `args` and `serverName`, and the row stops starting. Supply the
complete config, or use `REA_BUNDLE_LAUNCH=system` (above), which needs no patch at all.

Ghidra and the JDK are not read from your environment at launch: `setup.mjs` records their absolute paths in
`bundle.json` and the shim exports `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR` / `JAVA_HOME` from that record — which is why a
non-standard install location works without touching the row. To adopt an existing install, point
`GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR` / `JAVA_HOME` at it and run `node scripts/setup.mjs --reuse`: the manifest's probe checks
the candidate and falls back to a download when it does not match, so a wrong path is reported during setup
instead of failing later inside a tool call.

### One REA registration only

Upstream REA 6.5.0 can register itself with DSH:

```
rea setup --client dsh
```

That writes a row with `id: rea-mcp` and `serverName: rea` into `<DSH_HOME>/cordis.patch.yml`. This
bundle's row is `id: mcp-rea` with the same `serverName`, and DSH rejects the later of two entries
that share a server name — so which REA row survives depends on load order. **Use one, not both.**

Which one? Upstream's is the configuration-only route: it expects Node on REA's engines,
`rea-agents` reachable, and a Ghidra/JDK you provisioned yourself. This bundle is the
zero-dependency route: it fetches Node, REA, JDK and Ghidra on first run. The patch shape and the
`mcp__rea__*` surface are the same either way.

The shim reports the conflict on startup — `setup.mjs` records the DSH home it ran under in
`mirror.json`, and the mirrored copy reads that when the harness has stripped `DSH_*` from its
environment; `node bin/rea-shim.mjs --shim-status` lists it under `duplicateRegistration`.

## Verify

Ask for a `mcp__rea__*` call — `binary_session` reports the engine checks
(`configuration` / `installation` / `headless` / `native_decompiler` / `java`), all of which should be
`ok: true`. Then `open_binary` a PE, `binary_overview`, and `procedure_pseudo_code`.

Provisioning itself ends with three checks: `rea doctor --json` (reported, with unmet checks named), a
**Ghidra smoke import** that runs `rea analyze` on the JDK's own `bin/java` and fails the run when it
cannot import (`--skip-smoke` omits it), and the exact shim launch the MCP row will use. The smoke step
exists because `doctor` validates paths, versions and which Java would be chosen — it never imports a
binary, so a broken bridge or a mismatched native addon used to surface only as an MCP timeout.

**The first analysis of each new target is slow.** Measured here: 36 s for a small PE, 64 s for a 6 MB
DLL — every import starts a JVM and runs Ghidra's default auto-analysis. If the first
`open_binary` → `list_segments` on a large file times out, that is this cost and not a broken engine:
call it again and the open target answers immediately, because it keeps its ephemeral project.

## Scope and caveats

- REA exposes 229 tools at 6.8.0, so every session's tool list grows.
- Provisioning is honest about checksums: where a vendor publishes one it is pinned and verified; where none
  exists (jadx-headless-mcp, the apktool wrapper, Android platform-tools, the rolling "latest" URLs) the
  hash is **measured once and recorded**, and later drift is reported rather than silently accepted.
  `bundle.json` lists which components are in that state under `unverifiedChecksums`.
- Downloads are slow on some networks (measured 0.35–0.54 MiB/s from the GitHub release CDN here, so Ghidra
  alone takes ~25–45 min). Fetching is resumable on both routes: a partial `.part` is continued with a Range
  request, and a `.part` that already holds the whole file is verified and kept instead of re-fetched.
- Some REA tools launch processes, write files and access the network — DSH's permission policy applies.
  Analyse only artifacts you are authorized to inspect.
- The MCP child and the engines it launches are ordinary processes running as **you**. DSH's tool
  approvals govern what the model asks for, not what that child may read, write or send on its own;
  treat the plugin like any third-party code you install.
- On Linux, upstream's process-ownership checks need a **procps-compatible `ps`** on PATH; the
  Ghidra/JADX and firmware paths use it. A minimal image without it fails those tools, not the install.
- `scripts/setup.mjs` runs `npm install` for the REA CLI with `--ignore-scripts`: the published tarball
  carries no `node_modules`, so a dependency closure must be resolved, and package lifecycle scripts are
  skipped on purpose during provisioning. That step is also the **only** one that cannot use this bundle's
  own route/proxy resolution — npm reads `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY` and `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY` from the
  environment, so on a network that needs a mirror, set one of those before provisioning
  (`NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY=https://registry.npmmirror.com`). With `--offline` the step is refused outright
  instead of quietly going online.
- On POSIX, extraction falls back when the usual tools are missing: a zip is opened with `unzip`, then
  `python3 -m zipfile`, then the provisioned JDK's `jar`; a tarball with `tar`, then `python3`. A minimal
  image that has none of them fails with an explicit "no zip extractor available" line rather than a bare
  "extraction failed". This matters because Ghidra is a zip on every platform and `unzip` is not installed
  everywhere by default.

## Updating — three independent things

> **Two standing rules — for this release and for every later 2.x release.**
>
> `setup.mjs` reconciles the **bundle**, never the **plugin**: it reads the manifest of the plugin that is
> installed *right now*. Installed 2.0.9? setup provisions 6.5.0 even after a newer release exists. The package changes
> only through the market (or `npm i -g dsh-plugin-rea@<version>` / a `file:` reinstall); running setup more
> often never substitutes for that.
>
> **And nothing runs it for you.** A market install or update replaces the package and stops; the first
> `setup.mjs` — and one after every upgrade — is yours to run, from the plugin directory.
>
> 1. **The row executes a copy of this plugin's launcher.** `<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/rea-shim.mjs` is a
>    mirror made by setup, and a market upgrade replaces the package without replacing it — so the mirror can keep
>    running old code with **no symptom at all**. Since **2.0.8** the mirror compares itself with the launcher
>    recorded in `mirror.json` and re-execs the plugin's copy when the two differ (one hop, guarded by
>    `REA_BUNDLE_SHIM_REEXEC`). A mirror **older than 2.0.8 cannot do this**, so upgrading from **2.0.0–2.0.7**
>    still needs one `node scripts/setup.mjs`. `--shim-status` reports `mirror.stale`; `check-updates.ps1` says
>    when to re-run.
> 2. **The mirrored `scripts/setup.mjs` is a copy too, and it has no self-heal of its own.** Running setup from the
>    bundle root therefore executes the version from when the bundle was created, not the one you just installed.
>    Run it once **from the plugin directory** to refresh that copy. Since **2.0.9** the copy strips the UTF-8 BOM
>    from `mirror.json` / `bundle.json` exactly as the shim does, so a BOM-ed record no longer reads as "no record"
>    on the setup side (which used to re-mirror the previous manifest).

### Updating from the market

Update it where you installed it. Updating **to 2.0.5 or later** is routine; updating an installed 2.0.1–2.0.4
*through the in-app market* failed with this, three times on a healthy profile:

> dsh-plugin-rea 更新后缺少入口文件（package.json 的 main/exports 指向的文件不存在），且未能验证恢复原版本文件

That message is not about a broken tarball. On every update the market asks whether the new build's
`package.json` points at an entry file that exists (`hasLoadableEntry` in `dshmarket`), and rolls the build back
when the answer is false. A bundle may legitimately own no entry — but only if a package it *mounts* has one, and
the package this bundle mounts (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client`) ships inside the harness build rather than in
`node_modules`, so every location that test probes comes back empty. The 1.x and 2.0.x manifests also declared
no `main` at all, so the answer was false even though the profile was working; the rollback was then reported as
unverifiable for the same reason. Nothing in the profile was actually damaged — the update simply did not apply.

2.0.5 declares `main: ./index.mjs`. That file is a real, deliberately empty Cordis plugin: it registers nothing,
spawns nothing, touches no state — the working row is still inserted by `cordis.patch.yml` — and it exists so the
question "can this package load?" has an honest answer, and so `import 'dsh-plugin-rea'` resolves. On an older
version, update to `>=2.0.5`; if the market refuses before that version exists, install `dsh-plugin-rea@2.0.5`
(Desktop: through the plugin manager) instead of updating in place.

### Upgrading from 1.x

Install 2.x, then run provisioning **once** before restarting dsh:

```
node scripts/setup.mjs          # or: powershell -File scripts\rea-bundle-bootstrap.ps1 -Reuse
```

Why it matters: the 1.x row launched `rea mcp` from PATH, while the 2.x row launches
`<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/rea-shim.mjs` — a file only `setup.mjs` creates. Upgrade and restart
without provisioning and that row exits with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`: the harness stays up
(`failOnStartupError: false` is deliberate), but the `mcp__rea__*` tools are gone and you get **no
remediation message**, because the shim that prints one does not exist yet. After the setup run they are
back on the next start.

- **This plugin** never updates itself. Installed from a market? Update it there. Installed from a `file:`
  checkout? Overwrite the directory and reinstall.
- **The row runs a COPY of this plugin's launcher.** `<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/rea-shim.mjs` is a mirror
  made by setup, so a market upgrade replaces the package but not the file the row executes — until setup runs
  again. From **2.0.8** the mirror notices that the installed plugin ships a different launcher and re-execs it
  (one hop, guarded by `REA_BUNDLE_SHIM_REEXEC`), so upgrades carry. On an older version the mirror stays behind
  silently; `--shim-status` now reports `mirror.stale`, and `check-updates.ps1` says to re-run setup. If you are
  upgrading from 2.0.0–2.0.7, run `node scripts/setup.mjs` once after the upgrade.
- **The mirrored `scripts/setup.mjs` is a copy too.** A market upgrade replaces the package but not that copy,
  so a remediation command that points at `<DSH_HOME>/plugins/rea-bundle/scripts/setup.mjs` runs the setup from
  when the bundle was created — not the one you just installed. From **2.0.9** both the shim and setup strip a
  UTF-8 BOM from `mirror.json` / `bundle.json` (a BOM-ed record used to read as "no record" on the setup side,
  which re-mirrored the previous manifest). Running `node scripts/setup.mjs` once **from the plugin directory**
  refreshes that copy too.
- **Upgrading from `2.0.0-bundle.1`**: that release mirrored the shim and `setup.mjs` but not the manifest,
  and recorded nothing about the plugin checkout, so a bundle it provisioned cannot repair itself — its
  background provisioning dies on the missing manifest, invisibly, and its own lock suppresses retries for
  six hours. Re-run `node scripts/setup.mjs` **from the plugin directory** once; it re-mirrors all three
  files and writes the record that lets later runs find the checkout. `check-updates.ps1` reports this state.

#
# Registers the REA MCP server as mcp__rea__* and launches it through the
# bundle's own shim, which reads the machine-local state written by
# `scripts/setup.mjs` and exports exactly the variables REA reads.
#
# PORTABLE BY CONSTRUCTION — no machine path appears in this file.
#   * `command` is the running Node executable (`process.execPath`), so the
#     launcher needs no PATH entry and no shim resolution by the OS.
#   * `args[0]` is computed at boot from DSH_HOME, where setup mirrors the shim.
#   * FORWARD SLASHES ONLY in the JS string literals below. A single-quoted YAML
#     scalar keeps backslashes literal, and JavaScript then eats them: '\plugins'
#     is not "\plugins" but the BEL control character, '\rea-bundle' becomes a
#     carriage return and '\bin' a backspace, so the path is silently destroyed.
#     Forward slashes are accepted on Windows and are correct on POSIX, so one
#     expression serves every platform.
#   * `path`/`require` are not in scope for a `!!js` expression (`ctx` is the
#     loader scope), hence plain string concatenation.
#   * No DSH_HOME (undefined/absent/empty) falls back to the SAME rule the shim
#     and setup.mjs use — `<home>/.dsh` — never to the bare home directory.
#     Getting this wrong is silent: setup would mirror the shim into
#     `<home>/.dsh/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/` while the row looked for it one level
#     up, so the row could never start on a machine that merely happened to have
#     DSH_HOME unset.
#   * The home fallback mirrors Node's own `os.homedir()`: USERPROFILE, then
#     HOMEDRIVE+HOMEPATH (the shape a service account gets), then HOME. An
#     expression that checked only USERPROFILE and HOME produced `/.dsh/...` —

#

          # args[0] becomes an object the launcher cannot use. Quoting makes the
          # scalar unambiguous; the JS string literals inside use single quotes so
          # they cannot collide with the YAML ones.
          - !!js "(process.env.DSH_HOME && process.env.DSH_HOME.trim() !== '' ? process.env.DSH_HOME : (process.env.USERPROFILE || ((process.env.HOMEDRIVE || '') + (process.env.HOMEPATH || '')) || process.env.HOME || '') + '/.dsh') + '/plugins/rea-bundle/bin/rea-shim.mjs'"

          # for a plain Node host. Explicit is better than relying on this

  return cachedFacts

  res.writeHead(status, {

 *

 * yet REA needs absolute paths for every dependency. The shim is the seam: it

 *

 *              78 EX_CONFIG  bundle not provisioned (or unusable) — the row has
 *                            `failOnStartupError: false`, so the harness stays up
 *                            and the message is the operator's remediation.

import { spawn, spawnSync } from "node:child_process";
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { appendFileSync, existsSync, mkdirSync, readFileSync, rmSync, statSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import path from "node:path";
import process from "node:process";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";

const EX_CONFIG = 78;
const EX_USAGE = 64;
const HERE = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
const PLUGIN_ROOT = path.resolve(HERE, "..");

/**
 * JSON from disk, tolerating the UTF-8 BOM a Windows editor writes.
 *
 * `JSON.parse` rejects a leading BOM, and every caller here reads a parse
 * failure as "no record": a BOM would silently downgrade mirror.json to "no
 * plugin checkout" and bundle.json to "not provisioned". Measured while testing
 * this file — a hand-edited mirror.json written by Windows PowerShell behaved
 * exactly that way.
 */
function readJson(file) {
  const bytes = readFileSync(file);
  // UTF-16 is not hypothetical: Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes it by default
  // (`>` and `Out-File`), so a record a human produced that way used to read as
  // "no record" — the same silent downgrade the UTF-8 BOM fix addressed. Both
  // byte orders are handled; `scripts/setup.mjs` decodes exactly these shapes,
  // because two readers that disagree make one file mean two different things.
  if (bytes.length >= 2 && bytes[0] === 0xff && bytes[1] === 0xfe) {
    return JSON.parse(bytes.subarray(2).toString("utf16le"));
  }
  if (bytes.length >= 2 && bytes[0] === 0xfe && bytes[1] === 0xff) {
    const body = Buffer.from(bytes.subarray(2));
    body.swap16();
    return JSON.parse(body.toString("utf16le"));
  }
  return JSON.parse(bytes.toString("utf8").replace(/^\uFEFF/, ""));

  return path.join(homedir(), ".dsh");

  let value = null;

    if (typeof record?.dshHome === "string" && record.dshHome.trim() !== "" && path.isAbsolute(record.dshHome)) {

  } catch {
    return null;
  }
  const unquote = (value) => {
    const text = value.trim();
    // A quoted scalar ends at its own closing quote; everything after it is YAML
    // surface, not part of the value.
    const quoted = /^(['"])(.*?)\1/.exec(text);
    if (quoted) return quoted[2].trim();
    // A trailing comment needs whitespace before `#` (YAML), so `rea#1` is the
    // value while `rea # upstream` is not. Without this, the duplicate-row
    // diagnosis missed the exact row upstream writes by hand.
    return text.replace(/\s+#.*$/, "").trim();
  };
  // A row starts at `- id:`; the block runs to the next row, so a serverName can
  // never be attributed to a row that does not contain it.
  for (const block of text.split(/\r?\n(?=\s*-\s+id:\s*)/)) {
    const id = /^\s*-\s+id:\s*(.+?)\s*$/m.exec(block);
    const server = /^\s+serverName:\s*(.+?)\s*$/m.exec(block);
    if (!id || !server || unquote(server[1]) !== "rea") continue;
    const rowId = unquote(id[1]);
    if (rowId !== "mcp-rea") return { patch, id: rowId };
  }
  return null;
}

/**
 * The provisioning lock is a small JSON record: { state, pid, at, exit? }.
 * `state: "running"` is written when a run is started (setup's own pid once it
 * exists), and the failing run rewrites it as `state: "failed"` — it is kept on
 * purpose so a broken setup cannot be re-downloaded in a loop. A legacy
 * plain-number lock is still honoured as "running".
 */
const STALE_LOCK_MS = 6 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

function readLock(lock) {
  try {
    const raw = readFileSync(lock, "utf8").trim();
    if (raw.startsWith("{")) {
      const parsed = JSON.parse(raw);
      if (parsed && typeof parsed === "object") return parsed;
    }
    const at = Number(raw);
    return Number.isFinite(at) ? { state: "running", at } : null;
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

/** Is the process recorded in the lock still alive? null means "cannot tell". */
function pidAlive(pid) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(pid) || pid <= 0) return null;
  try {
    process.kill(pid, 0);
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    return error?.code === "ESRCH" ? false : null;
  }
}

/**
 * On first run there is nothing to launch. Provisioning is a long download, so
 * it is started detached: the harness may kill this row (or the whole session)
 * long before 800 MB arrive, and the downloader is resumable and idempotent, so
 * a killed attempt is simply continued on the next start.
 *
 * Set REA_BUNDLE_AUTO_PROVISION=0 to require an explicit `setup.mjs` run.
 * Returns { started, reason, logPath } — the caller words its message from
 * `reason`, because "provisioning started in the background" was also printed
 * for a lock left behind by a run that had already failed, and for one whose
 * process was long gone.
 */
function maybeAutoProvision(root) {
  if (process.env.REA_BUNDLE_AUTO_PROVISION === "0") return { started: false, reason: "disabled" };
  const setupScript = provisioningScript(root);
  if (!setupScript) return { started: false, reason: "no-setup" };
  const lock = path.join(root, "setup.lock");
  const logPath = path.join(root, "logs", "setup.log");
  if (existsSync(lock)) {
    // A crashed run must not wedge provisioning forever: honour the lock only
    // while it is fresh; setup removes it itself when it finishes cleanly.
    const record = readLock(lock);
    const age = record && Number.isFinite(record.at) ? Date.now() - record.at : Infinity;
    const fresh = Number.isFinite(age) && age < STALE_LOCK_MS;
    if (fresh && record?.state === "failed") {
      // The run gave up and left the lock behind so it would not be retried in a
      // loop. Claiming it is still provisioning was a six-hour lie: nothing runs,
      // and every restart repeated the sentence.
      return {
        started: false,
        reason: "last-run-failed",
        exit: record.exit,
        failedAt: record.at,
        ageMs: age,
        logPath,
      };
    }
    if (fresh) {
      const alive = pidAlive(record?.pid);
      if (alive !== false) return { started: false, reason: "in-flight", logPath, ageMs: age };
    }
    // Reached when the lock is older than the freshness window, or its holder is
    // gone and never wrote an outcome (harness restart, power loss, a kill): what
    // it records is not happening any more. This removal is the whole point of the
    // freshness rule — without it the exclusive create below failed with EEXIST
    // *forever*, auto-provisioning never ran again, and main() printed nothing at
    // all for that outcome. The lock's own "honour it only while it is fresh"
    // comment described behaviour the code did not have.
    try {
      rmSync(lock, { force: true });
    } catch {
      // A read-only bundle root (system-wide install, chmod 555) cannot drop the
      // stale lock either. Returning the same "cannot write here" outcome as the
      // exclusive create below keeps the row alive: an uncaught EACCES killed the
      // shim with a stack trace, which is louder than the old silence but just as
      // unable to start REA.
      return { started: false, reason: "unwritable", logPath };
    }
  }
  try {
    mkdirSync(path.join(root, "logs"), { recursive: true });
    // Exclusive create: check-then-write is not atomic, so two rows starting at
    // once could both decide to provision. EEXIST means another run owns it.
    writeFileSync(lock, JSON.stringify({ state: "running", pid: process.pid, at: Date.now() }), { flag: "wx" });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error?.code === "EEXIST") return { started: false, reason: "in-flight", logPath };
    /* a read-only bundle root must never break the harness */
    return { started: false, reason: "unwritable" };
  }
  let child;
  try {
    child = spawn(process.execPath, [setupScript, "--root", root], {
      detached: true,
      stdio: "ignore",
      windowsHide: true,
    });
  } catch {
    // The lock created a few lines up is ours. Leaving it as `running` with this
    // pid is a ghost a later start cannot tell from a real run — and if the pid is
    // reused inside the freshness window, provisioning stops for six hours.
    try {
      rmSync(lock, { force: true });
    } catch {
      /* advisory */
    }
    return { started: false, reason: "spawn-failed", logPath };
  }
  // A detached child that fails asynchronously (ENOENT, EACCES, ENOMEM) emits
  // 'error'; an EventEmitter with no listener throws, so the shim died with an
  // uncaught exception while the lock still named a live pid. Record the failure
  // instead: the next start then says "the last attempt failed" instead of
  // waiting out the window as "in flight".
  child.on("error", (error) => {
    try {
      writeFileSync(
        lock,
        JSON.stringify({
          state: "failed",
          pid: Number.isInteger(child.pid) ? child.pid : process.pid,
          at: Date.now(),
          exit: null,
          error: String(error?.code ?? error),
        }) + "\n",
      );
    } catch {
      /* the lock is advisory: the row keeps working without it */
    }
    try {
      appendFileSync(logPath, `rea-shim: provisioning could not be started: ${String(error?.message ?? error)}\n`);
    } catch {
      /* logging must never be fatal */
    }
  });
  child.unref();
  // Hand the lock to the detached downloader, so a later start that finds this
  // row dead still sees the run that is actually doing the work as alive.
  if (Number.isInteger(child.pid)) {
    try {
      writeFileSync(lock, JSON.stringify({ state: "running", pid: child.pid, at: Date.now(), supervisor: process.pid }));
    } catch {
      /* the lock is advisory: the row keeps working without it */
    }
  }
  return { started: true, reason: "started", logPath };
}

function fail(message, detail) {
  const lines = [
    "",
    "  dsh-plugin-rea (bundle): REA is not provisioned on this machine.",
    "",
    "  " + message,
  ];
  if (detail) lines.push("", "  detail: " + detail);
  // Point at the real checkout when the record allows it: running the mirrored
  // copy is fine, but it can only ever provision the manifest it was mirrored
  // with — and a bundle mirrored before the manifest travelled with it has no
  // usable copy at all, so the honest answer is then "run the plugin's own script".
  const root = bundleRoot();
  const setupScript = provisioningScript(root);
  lines.push(
    "",
    "  Finish setup with:",
    setupScript
      // `--root` is not decoration: a shim started with REA_BUNDLE_ROOT (or with
      // DSH_HOME unset in a row's scrubbed environment) resolves a root that
      // setup's own default need not agree with, and a remediation command that
      // provisions into another root leaves this row failing exactly as before.
      ? "    node \"" + setupScript + "\" --root \"" + root + "\""
      : "    node \"<installed plugin directory>/scripts/setup.mjs\" --root \"" + root + "\"",
  );
  if (!setupScript) {
    lines.push("", "  (Run it from the installed plugin directory: the copy in this bundle has no manifest.)");
  }
  lines.push(
    "",
    "  Then restart DSH (or reload the profile) so the MCP row reconnects.",
    "",
    "  The harness keeps running: this row declares failOnStartupError: false.",
    "",
  );
  process.stderr.write(lines.join("\n"));
  return EX_CONFIG;
}

function readBundleConfig(root) {
  const file = path.join(root, "bundle.json");
  if (!existsSync(file)) return { ok: false, code: "missing", file };
  let parsed;
  try {
    parsed = readJson(file);
  } catch (error) {
    return { ok: false, code: "malformed", file, detail: String(error && error.message) };
  }
  if (parsed === null || typeof parsed !== "object" || Array.isArray(parsed)) {
    return { ok: false, code: "malformed", file, detail: "bundle.json is not an object" };
  }
  return { ok: true, file, config: parsed };
}

/** Resolve the vendored REA entry, or report precisely what is missing. */
function resolveRea(config, root) {
  const paths = config.paths ?? {};
  const node = paths.node;
  // The fallback has to match where setup actually installs the package:
  // `npm install --prefix <root>/vendor` resolves into vendor/node_modules, so a
  // fallback without that segment named a directory that never exists. It only
  // fires when an older bundle.json has no paths.reaEntry — which is exactly when
  // a wrong fallback turns a usable install into "the vendored REA CLI is gone".
  const reaEntry = paths.reaEntry
    ?? path.join(root, "vendor", "node_modules", "rea-agents", "scripts", "rea.mjs");

  if (typeof node !== "string" || node.trim() === "") {
    return { ok: false, reason: "bundle.json has no paths.node" };
  }
  if (!existsSync(node)) {
    return { ok: false, reason: `the recorded Node runtime is gone: ${node}` };
  }
  if (!existsSync(reaEntry)) {
    return { ok: false, reason: `the vendored REA CLI is gone: ${reaEntry}` };
  }
  return { ok: true, node, reaEntry };
}

/**
 * Export only what REA actually reads, and only when the bundle recorded it.
 * An absent variable is better than a wrong one: REA then reports its own
 * availability with its own remediation text.
 */
function childEnvironment(config) {
  const env = { ...process.env };
  const paths = config.paths ?? {};

  const set = (name, value) => {
    if (typeof value === "string" && value.trim() !== "") env[name] = value;
  };

  // Analysis engines.
  set("GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR", paths.ghidra);
  set("JAVA_HOME", paths.jdk);
  // Optional providers/tools; wired only when the bundle provisioned them.
  set("REA_ADB_PATH", paths.adb);
  set("REA_APKTOOL_COMMAND", paths.apktoolCommand);
  set("REA_JADX_MCP_JAR", paths.jadxJar);
  set("REA_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE", paths.browser);
  set("REA_ILSPY_CMD_PATH", paths.ilspycmd);

  // Keep the vendored Node first for any grandchild the bridge may spawn.
  if (typeof paths.node === "string" && paths.node.trim() !== "") {
    const nodeDir = path.dirname(paths.node);
    const current = env.PATH ?? "";
    const parts = current.split(path.delimiter).filter((part) => part !== "");
    // Windows treats two spellings of one directory as equal, so a PATH already
    // carrying `C:\Program Files\nodejs` must not gain a second copy because the
    // vendored path is spelled `c:\program files\nodejs`. POSIX is case-sensitive
    // and keeps the exact comparison.
    const caseInsensitive = process.platform === "win32";
    const sameDir = (left, right) => {
      const a = path.resolve(left);
      const b = path.resolve(right);
      return caseInsensitive ? a.toLowerCase() === b.toLowerCase() : a === b;
    };
    if (!parts.some((part) => sameDir(part, nodeDir))) {
      env.PATH = [nodeDir, ...parts].join(path.delimiter);
    }
  }
  return env;
}

/**
 * Launch modes. 2.x exists to supply a runtime the machine does not have; when
 * the machine already has one, the honest thing to do is run it.
 *
 * The 1.x line was exactly that: `rea mcp` off PATH, user-managed Node and
 * Ghidra. So "use the system install" is not a new code path invented here — it
 * is the 1.x contract, reachable from the 2.x row. `auto` (the default) prefers
 * the system install and falls back to the provisioned bundle; `bundle` pins the
 * old behaviour; `system` insists (and fails loudly instead of provisioning
 * 800 MB behind an operator who asked for their own REA).
 */
const LAUNCH_MODES = ["auto", "system", "bundle"];

/**
 * How long a candidate may take to answer `--version`.
 *
 * Measured on a real npm-global install: `rea --version` through its `.cmd`
 * shim takes ~2.4 s cold (cmd.exe -> node -> the CLI's own module graph), and
 * 2.8-3.0 s with four probes in flight. A 3 s budget was therefore a coin flip:
 * half the runs rejected a perfectly good REA and silently fell back to the
 * bundle. 8 s leaves room for a slow disk and a loaded machine while still
 * bounding the one-off cost at startup.
 */
const PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS = 8_000;

/**
 * What the environment says about the launch mode.
 *
 * An unknown value is reported and treated as `auto`: the row is launched by
 * the harness with nobody watching stderr, so refusing to start over a typo
 * would read as "the plugin is broken". `auto` is the mode that still works.
 */
function launchPreference(env = process.env) {
  const raw = (env.REA_BUNDLE_LAUNCH ?? "").trim().toLowerCase();
  if (raw === "") return { value: "auto", invalid: null };
  return LAUNCH_MODES.includes(raw)
    ? { value: raw, invalid: null }
    : { value: "auto", invalid: raw };
}

/** True when `child` is `parent` or lives under it (case-insensitive on Windows). */
function isInside(child, parent) {
  const normalise = (value) => (process.platform === "win32" ? value.toLowerCase() : value);
  const target = normalise(path.resolve(child));
  const base = normalise(path.resolve(parent));
  if (target === base) return true;
  const relative = path.relative(base, target);
  return relative !== "" && !relative.startsWith("..") && !path.isAbsolute(relative);
}

/**
 * Executable names a REA install provides on this platform.
 *
 * npm's global install writes a shell script plus `.cmd`/`.ps1` shims on
 * Windows, and only the `.cmd` one is spawnable without a shell. `rea.exe` is
 * accepted for a native/standalone install.
 */
function systemReaNames(platform = process.platform) {
  return platform === "win32" ? ["rea.cmd", "rea.exe", "rea.bat"] : ["rea"];
}

/**
 * Every path worth probing, most explicit first.
 *
 * `REA_BUNDLE_SYSTEM_REA` names one binary outright — that is both the test
 * seam and a real operator need (an install that is not on the harness's PATH,
 * which on Desktop is not the user's shell PATH).
 */
function systemReaCandidates({ env = process.env, platform = process.platform } = {}) {
  const candidates = [];
  // The separator and the join follow the `platform` being RESOLVED, not the one
  // this process happens to run on. The comment below always claimed the tests
  // could exercise both shapes on one machine; with `path.delimiter` that was
  // false — a POSIX host split a Windows PATH (`;`) on `:`, produced drive-letter
  // fragments, and every candidate pointed at nothing. Production is unaffected
  // (the two agree there), which is exactly why the seam had to be real.
  const api = platform === "win32" ? path.win32 : path.posix;
  const delimiter = platform === "win32" ? ";" : ":";
  const explicit = (env.REA_BUNDLE_SYSTEM_REA ?? "").trim();
  if (explicit !== "") candidates.push(api.resolve(explicit));
  const searchPath = env.PATH ?? env.Path ?? "";
  for (const raw of searchPath.split(delimiter)) {
    // A quoted PATH entry (`PATH="C:\Program Files\v66";…`) is legal in Windows
    // environments and `path.join` would treat the quotes as part of the name, so
    // the install would be invisible. A relative entry is skipped rather than
    // resolved: its meaning depends on the cwd THIS process happens to have, and
    // a candidate found that way would be launched by a path that means something
    // else to whoever reads the status report.
    const dir = raw.trim().replace(/^"(.*)"$/, "$1");
    if (dir === "" || !api.isAbsolute(dir)) continue;
    for (const name of systemReaNames(platform)) candidates.push(api.join(dir, name));
  }
  const seen = new Set();
  return candidates.filter((candidate) => {
    // Keyed on the platform being RESOLVED, not on the one this process happens
    // to run: the tests pass `platform` to exercise both shapes on one machine.
    const key = platform === "win32" ? candidate.toLowerCase() : candidate;
    if (seen.has(key)) return false;
    seen.add(key);
    return true;
  });
}

/**
 * Kill a process and its children.
 *
 * `spawnSync`'s timeout kills only the process it started — for a `.cmd` shim
 * that is cmd.exe, and the `node` running inside it keeps the inherited stdio
 * handles open and keeps working. Taskkill's `/T` is the one portable-enough way
 * to get the tree on Windows; POSIX uses the process itself (the candidate is a
 * shebang script there, so there is no intermediate shell).
 */
function killTree(pid, platform = process.platform) {
  if (typeof pid !== "number" || pid <= 0) return;
  try {
    if (platform === "win32") {
      const taskkill = path.join(process.env.SystemRoot ?? process.env.SYSTEMROOT ?? "C:\\Windows", "System32", "taskkill.exe");
      spawnSync(taskkill, ["/pid", String(pid), "/T", "/F"], {
        stdio: "ignore",
        windowsHide: true,
        timeout: 5_000,
      });
      return;
    }
    try {
      process.kill(pid, "SIGKILL");
    } catch {
      /* already gone */
    }
  } catch {
    /* best effort: a failed cleanup must not change the verdict */
  }
}

/** True when the path is a regular file (a directory named `rea.cmd` is not). */
function isFileSync(file) {
  try {
    return statSync(file).isFile();
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

/** A command line that survives `cmd /c` on Windows: quoted, quotes doubled. */
function cmdQuote(value) {
  return `"${String(value).replace(/"/g, '""')}"`;
}

/**
 * The shell used to run a `.cmd`/`.bat` candidate.
 *
 * Absolute on purpose: `spawn(comspec())` is resolved against the CHILD's PATH,
 * and an MCP row inherits a scrubbed environment. A machine with a working REA
 * but a PATH that does not include System32 would then be judged "no REA",
 * which is precisely the wrong answer for the feature that exists to find it.
 */
function comspec() {
  const fromEnv = process.env.ComSpec ?? process.env.COMSPEC;
  // A ComSpec that names nothing is a real (if unusual) state, and trusting it
  // would judge every `.cmd` REA "spawn-failed" — i.e. report the machine as
  // having no REA because its shell pointer is broken. Fall back to the path
  // Windows itself would use.
  if (typeof fromEnv === "string" && fromEnv.trim() !== "" && isFileSync(fromEnv)) return fromEnv;
  const systemRoot = process.env.SystemRoot ?? process.env.SYSTEMROOT ?? "C:\\Windows";
  return path.join(systemRoot, "System32", "cmd.exe");
}

/**
 * Ask a candidate whether it is a working REA.
 *
 * A file existing on PATH is not the same as a working install: npx leftovers,
 * half-removed globals and a shim whose Node is gone all sit on PATH and all
 * fail at once. One bounded `--version` separates them, and a slow or hanging
 * answer counts as "not usable" — the fallback (the bundle) still works, while
 * delegating to a broken binary would take the tools down with it.
 *
 * Two things here are not incidental:
 *
 *  * The probe runs with `REA_BUNDLE_DELEGATED=1`. A candidate that is itself a
 *    wrapper around this shim would otherwise be probed by a nested shim that
 *    probes the wrapper — measured: a process chain that keeps respawning
 *    itself. The flag makes the nested run take the bundle path and return.
 *  * It is asynchronous, not `spawnSync` with a timeout. `spawnSync` reaps the
 *    child it started, and its timeout kills only that child: for a `.cmd` shim
 *    that means cmd.exe dies while the REA inside it keeps running and holds
 *    the pipes. Killing the TREE is only possible while the parent is alive,
 *    which means owning the wait ourselves.
 */
function probeRea(file, { platform = process.platform, timeout = PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS } = {}) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    // `existsSync` says nothing about the shape: a DIRECTORY named `rea.cmd`
    // exists, fails to spawn, and would be reported as a broken install instead
    // of as a name collision. Only a regular file is a candidate.
    if (!isFileSync(file)) {
      resolve({ ok: false, reason: "not a file" });
      return;
    }
    const useShell = platform === "win32" && /\.(cmd|bat)$/i.test(file);
    // `REA_BUNDLE_AUTO_PROVISION=0` is part of the same guard: if the candidate
    // turns out to be a wrapper around THIS shim, the nested run must not start
    // an 800 MB provisioning job just because a probe asked it for a version.
    const env = { ...process.env, REA_BUNDLE_DELEGATED: "1", REA_BUNDLE_AUTO_PROVISION: "0" };
    // `cmd /d /s /c "<line>"`: Windows only. Two details are load-bearing.
    // `/s` strips the first and last quote, so the whole line is quoted; and the
    // arguments are passed VERBATIM, because Node otherwise backslash-escapes the
    // quotes it sees and cmd.exe does not understand `\"` — every candidate then
    // answers "exit 1", which reads as "no REA on this machine".
    const child = useShell
      ? spawn(comspec(), ["/d", "/s", "/c", `"${[cmdQuote(file), "--version"].join(" ")}"`], {
          env,
          stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"],
          windowsHide: true,
          windowsVerbatimArguments: true,
        })
      : spawn(file, ["--version"], { env, stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"], windowsHide: true });
    let output = "";
    let settled = false;
    let timer = null;
    const finish = (result) => {
      if (settled) return;
      settled = true;
      if (timer !== null) clearTimeout(timer);
      resolve(result);
    };
    timer = setTimeout(() => {
      killTree(child.pid, platform);
      finish({ ok: false, reason: "timeout" });
    }, timeout);
    // `--version` prints one line. A damaged or hostile candidate on PATH can
    // print without end for the whole timeout, so the accumulator is capped and
    // the tree is killed once it trips: an unbounded string here is a memory
    // lever a stranger controls.
    const OUTPUT_LIMIT = 64 * 1024;
    const collect = (chunk) => {
      if (settled || output.length >= OUTPUT_LIMIT) return;
      output += String(chunk);
      if (output.length > OUTPUT_LIMIT) {
        output = output.slice(0, OUTPUT_LIMIT);
        killTree(child.pid, platform);
        finish({ ok: false, reason: "output exceeded 64 KiB" });
      }
    };
    child.stdout.on("data", collect);
    child.stderr.on("data", collect);
    child.on("error", () => finish({ ok: false, reason: "spawn-failed" }));
    child.on("close", (code) => {
      if (code !== 0) {
        finish({ ok: false, reason: `exit ${String(code)}` });
        return;
      }
      // A REA install prints its version. Anything else (a shim that swallowed
      // the flag, an unrelated program that shares the name) is not a usable CLI.
      const version = /\b(\d+\.\d+\.\d+(?:-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?)\b/.exec(output.trim())?.[1] ?? null;
      finish(version === null
        ? { ok: false, reason: "no version in --version output" }
        : { ok: true, version });
    });
  });
}

/**
 * The system REA this machine already has, or why it was rejected.
 *
 * Candidates inside this bundle or this checkout are skipped: a REA that the
 * provisioner installed is the `bundle` mode, and delegating to it would be a
 * loop through a path the bundle already covers.
 */
async function detectSystemRea({ env = process.env, platform = process.platform, root, pluginRoot = PLUGIN_ROOT } = {}) {
  const rejected = [];
  let profiled = 0;
  const explicit = (env.REA_BUNDLE_SYSTEM_REA ?? "").trim();
  // Probing costs a process start per candidate, and a row has to answer before
  // its tools exist. The first existing entry is what the shell would run, so a
  // couple of fallbacks is plenty; a machine whose first three `rea`s are all
  // broken is a repair job, not something this decision should keep paying for.
  const MAX_PROBES = 3;
  for (const candidate of systemReaCandidates({ env, platform })) {
    if (isInside(candidate, root) || isInside(candidate, pluginRoot)) {
      // A REA the provisioner installed is `bundle` mode; delegating to it would
      // be a loop back into the thing this decision is choosing between.
      if (rejected.length < 8) rejected.push({ file: candidate, reason: "inside the bundle" });
      continue;
    }
